displayContract.byline: Assessments made by 5.6 Sol. — Rubric: Slugfester Reassessment Rubric v2.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that bodily resurrection merits acceptance as the best historical explanation only if a carefully qualified cumulative case makes death, bodily absence, early embodied belief, and appearances jointly more expected than they are under the strongest nonresurrection alternatives.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the closing by qualifying its conclusion and defining the comparative burden across the principal evidential strands.

premises.text: Roman execution practice, the preceding trauma, early death proclamation, and the reported official confirmation should be treated as mutually relevant but not automatically independent evidence, yielding a strong case-specific probability of death without invoking universal medical agreement.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the death argument by narrowing its medical claim and directly incorporating the rapid-death objection.

premises.text: The empty tomb should rest on a cumulative assessment of burial identification, Jerusalem proclamation, hostile body-removal explanation, and embodied resurrection semantics, with each indicator discounted where its provenance or dependence remains uncertain.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the empty-tomb inference by making access, identification, provenance, and evidential dependence explicit.

premises.text: Early appearance testimony most securely establishes sincere and transformative experiences; a bodily interpretation becomes stronger only when that testimony is combined with embodied resurrection language and bodily absence, not from sincerity or conversion alone.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the appearance route by separating sincerity from phenomenology and specifying the additional bridge to physicality.

premises.text: Early Pauline and pre-Pauline formulas should be cited individually and evaluated for dating, provenance, and bodily meaning; chronology supports the case only when the formulas themselves connect the deceased Jesus with the one proclaimed raised.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the early-tradition argument by requiring textual demonstration rather than relying mainly on reference counts.

premises.text: Explanatory comparison should test resurrection, survival, rescue, bereavement or revelatory experiences, spiritual vindication, and narrative development by common criteria: coverage, evidential fit, auxiliary assumptions, source chronology, and compatibility with acknowledged uncertainty.

novelty.explanation: This introduces an explicit common-criteria comparison that neither participant fully articulated in the locked moves.

conclusion.text: If the death, bodily-absence, early embodied-belief, and appearance strands retain substantial support after dependence and source development are discounted, bodily resurrection can be judged the strongest presented explanation, though the historical inference remains probabilistic and contestable.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the affirmative conclusion by making it conditional, comparative, and proportionate to residual historical uncertainty.

newArguments.title: Correlated-evidence sensitivity test
newArguments.text: A stronger affirmative case would explicitly model evidential dependence. The hostile explanation may depend on the same tradition as the empty-tomb narrative, and bodily resurrection semantics may not independently prove a known burial place. The case should therefore ask whether its conclusion survives after correlated indicators receive reduced weight. If death, bodily absence, early proclamation, and sincere appearances still converge after that discount, the inference gains credibility precisely because it does not depend on counting every report as independent confirmation.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a sensitivity analysis for correlated evidence, a methodological line absent from the participant moves.

newArguments.title: Discriminating-predictions comparison
newArguments.text: Rather than claiming that every alternative fails, the affirmative could identify observations on which the accounts differ. Survival predicts a severely injured continuing Jesus and requires a pathway through custody; purely visionary accounts do not naturally predict bodily absence; pure literary development weakens expectations of a very early identified resurrection proclamation. None of those contrasts is decisive alone, but jointly they permit a transparent comparison. Resurrection earns preference only if it predicts the combined pattern with fewer unsupported auxiliary assumptions than each serious rival.

novelty.explanation: This extends the explanatory comparison beyond rescue and supplies the explicit discriminating criteria missing from the closing.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that the historical record can support early sincere resurrection belief while still failing to discriminate sufficiently between physical resurrection and combinations of uncertain death, revelatory experience, spiritual vindication, and later narrative physicalization.

novelty.explanation: This extends the negative's insufficiency thesis while acknowledging the strongest secure affirmative evidence about early sincere belief.

premises.text: The death premise should be evaluated cumulatively, but Mark's rapid timeline, Pilate's reported surprise, and the later emergence of decisive physical details leave some case-specific uncertainty that general crucifixion lethality alone cannot remove.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the death challenge by acknowledging the affirmative convergence while preserving the particularized textual uncertainty.

premises.text: Early resurrection language may have bodily associations without itself documenting an identifiable empty tomb, numerical continuity with the corpse, or tactile encounters; those propositions require separate historical bridges rather than semantic assumption.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the spiritual reading by conceding bodily associations while distinguishing them from stronger historical entailments.

premises.text: Paul's placement of his revelatory experience beside earlier appearances does not prove identical phenomenology, but it demonstrates that list membership alone cannot establish that every recipient encountered a tangible, locally present body.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the Pauline argument by avoiding the unwarranted inference from common listing to identical experiential mode.

premises.text: Increasing physical specificity across later narratives is evidence of development only after literary dependence, genre, authorial purpose, and possible clarification are assessed; nevertheless, it limits using later detail as straightforward independent confirmation.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the development argument by distinguishing elaboration from invention while retaining its evidential consequence.

premises.text: Historical non-establishment does not require proving a complete rescue or survival narrative; it requires showing that key evidence has similar likelihood under multiple live accounts after reasonable uncertainty and source dependence are recognized.

novelty.explanation: This extends the burden argument by formally separating an underdetermination defense from a positive rescue theory.

conclusion.text: Unless the evidence independently secures death, bodily absence, and specifically physical appearances while distinguishing early content from later elaboration, the proportionate historical conclusion is that bodily resurrection remains insufficiently established, not that a particular alternative is proved.

novelty.explanation: This extends the negative conclusion by stating the precise evidential conditions and avoiding any stronger contrary historical claim.

newArguments.title: Incremental-content audit
newArguments.text: The negative could separate the tradition into propositions and date the earliest secure support for each: Jesus died, God raised him, appearances were reported, the burial place was empty, and encounters involved tangible bodily interaction. Early support for the first three would not automatically backdate the final two. This incremental audit avoids treating every later detail as invention while still asking whether the evidence needed for physical resurrection appears only after additional narrative development. The motion fails if its distinctively physical components remain later or independently uncertain.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a proposition-by-proposition chronology rather than treating bodily tradition as one indivisible historical package.

newArguments.title: Likelihood-equivalence challenge
newArguments.text: The negative need not show that one naturalistic theory explains everything. It can ask whether crucial observations are approximately as expected under more than one account: sincere experiences under revelation or grief, early raising language under vindication, and increasing physical detail under clarification or development. Where rival accounts predict an observation comparably well, that observation contributes little discriminatory force. The affirmative must therefore identify evidence whose probability differs materially across the alternatives, rather than relying primarily on the number or vividness of mutually compatible facts.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a likelihood-based account of underdetermination that strengthens the burden analysis without adopting a single rival narrative.
